The most striking clinical feature of our patient was the presence of painful spasms of the right thigh which occurred spontaneously or were induced by voluntary action or unexpected noises.

our patient had anti-GAD antibodies in serum (109 U/mL; radioimmunoassay) and oligoclonal bands in the cerebrospinal fluid that, even if not pathognomonic, are widely reported in stiff-person syndrome.
Continuous motor unit activity at rest was recorded by surface electrodes and then confirmed by needle EMG in the paraspinal cervical and thigh muscles.
Extensive investigation, including the imaging of the whole neuraxis, failed to disclose any abnormality.

Limb dystonia is unlikely, because dystonic spasms are generally less painful and not stimulus-sensitive. Spasticity can be excluded, because there were no upper motor neuron signs and central motor conduction time was normal.

Routine nerve conduction studies were performed in ulnar, peroneal, and sural nerves on the right side. ... Somatosensory evoked potentials and motor evoked potentials did not detect any sign of long tract involvement.

Cutaneomuscular/exteroceptive reflexes were of an abnormally low threshold. Stimulus at three times the sensory threshold gave consistent short and long latency responses in tibialis anterior, gastrocnemius, vastus lateralis, biceps femoris.

extractions.value: Patient had insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus and mild polyneuropathy (absent sural sensory response, slowed peroneal conduction velocity). Spasms could be induced by transcranial magnetic stimulation and electrical shocks at the ankle. The authors classify the case as focal stiff-person syndrome with proximal muscle and cervical paraspinal involvement.
